title: A returns policy written like a person
metaTitle: Returns copy a customer can use
excerpt: Say the return window, who pays for the label, and how to start. Legal can review the long document. The person holding the package still has to act on three plain sentences.
alt: Clothes on wooden hangers suspended from a white branch against a plain wall. The arrangement is plain enough to read, which is what a returns policy needs.
caption: A plain arrangement you can read at a glance. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should a returns policy say first?
faqs.answer: Say how long the customer has, who pays to send the item back, and how to start. Put those three sentences on the product page and in the receipt, and let the longer page hold the exceptions. A footer link alone is where the policy goes unread.

faqs.question: Can a strict policy still be clear?
faqs.answer: Yes. A short window, a customer-paid label, or a final-sale item can be honest if it is stated before purchase, next to the price. The defect is hiding the rule in a document nobody opens, then enforcing it after the parcel arrives.

faqs.question: Where should legal review sit?
faqs.answer: Counsel, or a careful founder, should check claims you cannot afford to get wrong, then leave the shop free to rewrite the rest into speech. Bring the reviewer the three sentences the customer will use, not only the master document. If a person cannot act on them, the page is not done.

markdown:
A returns policy UX is the short version a customer can use: the window, who pays to send it back, and how to start. Legal can review the long document. The person holding the package still has to be able to read the decision without a law degree.

Put that short version where the purchase happens, on the product page and again in the bag. A policy that exists only as a footer link is a policy people meet after they already feel misled.

## The three facts, in plain sentences

Write three sentences before you write the exceptions.

How long they have. “You can start a return within 30 days of delivery.” Name the event you count from. Delivery, purchase, and the end of the month are different clocks. Use one.

Who pays. “We pay return shipping on defects. You pay return shipping on a change of mind.” If the return shipping comes out of the refund, say that in the same breath. A refund that quietly shrinks is the moment trust drops.

How to start. “Reply to your receipt, or use the link in it. We’ll send a label or the address.” Name the path that actually works in your shop. If returns are an email to a person, say that. If they are a portal, link it. “Contact us” with no address is not a start.

Baymard Institute’s page on [cart abandonment statistics](https://baymard.com/lists/cart-abandonment-rate) lists reasons US online shoppers give, and a shopper can name more than one. A returns policy that was not satisfactory sits at 13 percent, beside extra costs at 40 percent and the inability to see the total up front at 12 percent. The figure is a reason to put the three sentences next to the price. It is not a quota. Your policy can be strict. It cannot be hidden.

The [W3C’s WCAG 2 overview](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) describes an understandable guideline set: people should be able to grasp the content and how to operate it. A returns page written as a single block of defined terms fails that test even when a lawyer has approved every clause. Hanabi does not certify the page. The writing standard is still the right one. Short sentences. Defined words. The action named.

## What legal review is for

Counsel, or a careful founder acting as counsel, should check the claims you cannot afford to get wrong. Warranties, health claims, final-sale items, and anything regulated. That review should mark the sentences that must remain, and then let the shop rewrite everything around them into speech.

Bring the reviewer the three sentences, not only the master document. Ask whether a customer could act on them. If the answer is no, the document is not done. A PDF that wins an argument and loses the inbox is an expensive PDF.

Keep a change log in plain language when the window or the payer changes. “From June 1, change-of-mind returns are 14 days, and the customer pays the label.” People who bought under the old rule deserve the old rule, or an explicit note in the receipt about which rule applied. Surprise is the defect, not the existence of a limit.

Final sale is allowed when it is specific. Mark the product on its page, in the same block as the price, and repeat it in the bag. A final-sale rule that appears only in a policy the buyer never opened will be disputed, and you will spend the refund anyway in the time you spend arguing.

## Where the short version sits

On the product page, under the price or beside shipping. Two lines and a link named “Returns” that goes to the full page. The link text should say what they will get. “30-day returns. We pay the label on defects.” Then the link for the rest.

In the bag, the same two lines near the total. People re-read cost and risk together. Do not invent a friendlier policy at this step than the one you will honor.

In the receipt email, repeat the window and the start path. This is the document they will search for in three weeks. If the email says “see our website for returns,” you have moved the work back onto them at the moment they are most willing to follow a link. Put the link, and put the deadline date if you can compute it.

On the returns page itself, open with the three sentences. Then the exceptions: hygiene, personalized goods, worn items, international labels, exchanges versus refunds. Use headings a person can scan. A wall of text is where the true exception goes to hide, including from your own support team.

Support macros should quote the same sentences. If the inbox says “we usually do 30 days” and the page says 14, you have two policies. Pick one and make the macro match the page the same day.

## Exchanges, refunds, and the money

Say what they receive. A refund to the original payment method, store credit, or an exchange. If you default to credit, say that before they start, not in the confirmation after they have already packed the box. Baymard’s extra-cost reason is about surprise charges. A refund that becomes a gift card is a surprise of the same family.

Say when the money moves. “We refund within five business days of the return arriving at our studio.” “The label is emailed within one business day.” Windows you can keep are better than “as soon as possible,” which every angry customer will interpret as yesterday.

If you deduct shipping they already paid, or a restocking fee, the amount belongs in the short version. A fee that shows up as a smaller deposit is the story they will tell about you. Name the number.

International returns need one honest line. If you cannot offer a label, say who pays duties and whether the refund includes the original shipping. If you cannot accept returns from outside your country, say that on the product page for those shoppers, not after the parcel has crossed a border.

## Defects versus a change of mind

These are different operations, and the page should treat them as different. A defect is your cost: label, replacement or refund, and a tone that does not make them prove they are reasonable. Ask for a photo if you need it to send the right replacement. Do not ask for a photo as a ritual to slow them down.

A change of mind can be stricter. The item unworn, tags on, their label. Say the condition in concrete terms. “Unworn, with tags, in the original pack” is checkable. “In saleable condition” is an argument.

Do not make the defect path look like the change-of-mind path. If both start at the same form, the first question should split them. People who received a broken object should not have to read the rules for people who changed their mind.

Ballarat Box Sports, a public community sports brand site, and a fashion shop do not need the same exception list. A team uniform and a linen shirt fail in different ways. Write the exceptions for the objects you sell. A template policy from a platform is a draft, not a voice.

## The page has to be operable

The start path should work on a phone, because that is where they will read the receipt. A form with twelve fields to request a label will be abandoned, and then they will write to you anyway, angrier. Ask for the order number and the reason. You already have the address.

Errors should name the field. If the order number does not match, say so, and say where to find it in the receipt. A generic failure sends them to a new email thread that your team has to untangle by hand.

If a person must print a label, say that, and also offer a QR or a code the carrier can scan from the phone when the carrier allows it. Many people do not have a printer. A policy that assumes a home office will fail in apartments.

The confirmation after they submit should say what happens next and when. “You’ll get a label by tomorrow evening. Pack the item with the form. Drop it at any of these locations.” That is the end of the anxiety. “Request received” is the beginning of a new one.

Keep a human available for the cases the form cannot see: a missing delivery, a wrong item, a gift they do not want to reveal a price on. Put that address on the page. A careful shop is allowed to be strict and still be reachable.

## Write it, then read it as the customer

Read the short version aloud. If you stumble, the sentence is too long. Then ask someone who did not write it to explain the policy back to you in their own words. If they miss who pays, the page missed it too.

Check three products: a normal one, a final-sale one, and a preorder if you sell those. The short version on each should differ only where the rule differs. Then place an order, open the receipt, and start a return you intend to cancel. The path you just walked is the policy. The document is the backup.

When the return is done, the next structural question for many growing shops is who the site is even for. Retail buyers and wholesale buyers do not share a product page cleanly. [Wholesale versus retail on one domain](/blog/wholesale-versus-retail-on-one-domain) is the piece that follows, because a policy written for one of them will confuse the other if both are forced through the same door.

If you want to see how a shop can carry this kind of plain-language policy next to the work, look through [Hanabi’s selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works). The public projects are the evidence of how a storefront gets written, not a promise that every brand uses the same window.
